name: Liam Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a haul truck at a large mine, carrying rock along a marked route to the crusher. The radio starts before dawn, and I still double-check the turning point because I'm fairly new and the old hands know the ground better. I like the quiet stretch after the first load; I don't like the dust that follows me home. I'm 43, my partner Sam works at a school kitchen, and our two children are in school too. We have a mortgage, though we've managed to keep more than six months of bills in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the other drivers that a bit of office software isn't going to steer my truck round a blind bend. We should still be paid for the shift and allowed to stop when a route is unsafe. I don't use AI myself. The paper route sheet works for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm glad the small changes leave the pay scale alone. The mortgage is manageable on my higher mine wage, and our savings could cover more than half a year if something went wrong. Sam's school kitchen hours are less secure, so I won't call the household untouchable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving my assigned route and doing the brake check with the morning crew. This month I'd leave the household savings where they are and go through Sam's kitchen rota with Sam before agreeing to any new monthly bill. In the first year I'd keep the same work pattern unless the mine actually changes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly settled about my own job in this picture. I still glance at the kitchen rota because one missing week there changes our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by one missing week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam has had holiday weeks when the kitchen wanted fewer staff. My mine wage covered the bills, but the children noticed we skipped the swimming trip we'd promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not for a small time saving. I want the route on paper where I can mark a blocked lane and show the next driver exactly what I saw.

say: I would tell drivers **minor office software** cannot steer my haul truck around a blind bend.
I want the right to **stop an unsafe route** and keep shift pay.
think: My **mine wage and savings** make the mortgage manageable if my own work holds.
Sam’s **kitchen hours** can vary, so the whole household is less certain.
do: Keep driving my **assigned route** and checking brakes with the morning crew.
Review Sam’s **kitchen rota** before agreeing to any new monthly bill.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a watchful eye on Sam’s hours.
S0.quote: The paper route sheet works for me.
fieldNote: Liam sees little direct threat to his **haul truck work** from minor office automation.
His stronger savings cushion matters, but **variable kitchen hours** remain a household concern.

steps.text: Keep driving the assigned haul route and checking brakes each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the pit meeting I'd say the company should show workers which buying and dispatch jobs software is taking. I'm not volunteering to have an algorithm assign trips without anyone checking road conditions. Our union can ask for the records before the first roster is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know dispatch might need fewer people when planning gets automated, and that could change the number of trips we get. My truck still needs a person for now, but mine managers have a way of calling fewer shifts an efficiency. I could move to another nearby mine if it happened; there are plenty, yet I'd rather keep this wage and the short drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd attend the next union meeting and ask our representative for the proposed dispatch and driver rosters. I'd keep taking my truck shifts while the changes are debated. If my hours drop in the first year, I'd send applications to two nearby pits and cut the children's paid weekend outings until a new wage is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cross at decisions made far from the road, and nervous about the hours. Having other mines nearby gives me a way out, but starting again at junior grade would still sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the representative to obtain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old and proposed rosters, with actual driving hours beside them. I don't want a speech about protecting jobs if nobody can show whose Friday shift vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which outings would stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cinema and the climbing place charge for all four of us. We'd still go to the free park; the children don't need to pay for every Saturday.

say: I would ask for the **dispatch and buying changes** to be shown to workers.
Our union should get **roster records** before shifts are cut.
think: Faster planning could mean **fewer truck hours**, even while people still drive.
Other mines offer work, but I could lose my **higher wage** and short commute.
do: Attend the **union meeting** and request old and proposed rosters.
Keep driving while the change is debated, then apply to **nearby pits** if hours fall.
Cut **paid weekend outings** until replacement wages are certain.
feel: **Cross** about distant decisions and nervous about hours.
S1.quote: I don't want a speech about protecting jobs if nobody can show whose Friday shift vanished.
fieldNote: His collective response is about **verifiable rosters**, not automatic faith in the union.
The many nearby mines provide options, while losing his current **higher wage** would hurt.

steps.text: Attend the next union meeting and request old and proposed rosters
Keep taking assigned truck shifts while changes are debated
Apply to two nearby pits if driving hours drop
Stop paid cinema and climbing outings until wages settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union we need two dates written on one page: thinking AI in 2028 and truck-driving robots around 2031. No one should be told the truck job is safe merely because the first machine sits in an office. I'd ask for a paid route into another job before the trucks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frankly, I don't trust myself to pick up some new screen trade in two years. I have never used AI, and I'm still learning parts of this mine. Our savings buy us time, not a second career. If autonomous trucks work as well as people in 2031, my higher wage could vanish while the mortgage stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the dates to the next union meeting and press for a written plan for drivers. I'd keep driving and save part of each monthly wage in a separate job-loss account from now on. In 2029, the year after thinking AI, I'd watch the driver roster and apply to nearby pits still hiring people. If robots really take the trucks in 2031, I'd use the savings while looking for paid work, not wait at home for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel angry and pretty scared, although I'm not frozen. The children are young enough to ask whether we must leave the house, and I can't answer that confidently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apply to other pits if robots can arrive there too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might only buy a few paid months. Those months would cover the mortgage while Sam and I decide whether I need a different kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're keeping the house for now and the adults are checking other jobs. I'd rather give them a small truthful answer than say everything is fine when I don't know.

say: I would demand **two clear dates**: thinking AI in 2028 and capable truck robots around 2031.
I would ask the union for a **paid driver transition** before robots arrive.
think: My limited screen skills make a **two-year switch** hard to trust.
Savings buy time, but my **higher wage** could disappear while the mortgage remains.
do: Press the **union** for a written driver plan.
Keep driving and add monthly wages to a **job-loss account**.
Check 2029 rosters and apply to **nearby pits** still hiring drivers.
feel: **Angry and scared**, while able to take some steps.
S2.quote: Our savings buy us time, not a second career.
fieldNote: He distinguishes the **2028 desk change** from the later threat to physical driving.
His household cushion creates options, but replacing a **higher mine wage** remains difficult.

steps.text: Press the union for a written transition plan for drivers
Keep driving assigned truck shifts before robots arrive
Transfer part of each monthly wage to a separate job-loss account
Apply to nearby pits still hiring drivers after checking 2029 rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine has five years to bargain over real wages and jobs, not just another safety leaflet. Thinking AI comes in 2031, while robots that can drive a haul truck as well as me arrive around 2034. I'd want drivers at the table before the order is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when the thinking system comes and 51 when the robots come, I may still owe on the house. The children will be older and might need money for training or travel, so the family cannot simply live off savings. Five years lets me weigh nearby mines and perhaps a hands-on trade, but I don't suddenly become keen on classroom software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to negotiate paid release time for mechanical training and a wage floor for drivers moved off trucks. If that paid course is secured, I'd enrol while keeping my current shifts. In 2032 I'd ask the mine for the driver headcount and apply to other nearby mines if ours is shrinking. By 2034 I'd look for a paid maintenance job if the truck seats go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier than in the two-year version because there is time to bargain. I still dislike being told to retrain as if the mortgage will pause during a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What training would you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Basic mechanical inspection under a qualified fitter, with wages while I learn. I would not sign up for an unpaid course that ends with a certificate and no employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wage floor mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a driver moves to inspection, the first year's pay should not fall off a cliff. I want that in writing before anyone calls the move a fair offer.

say: I would say **five years** gives the mine time to negotiate wages and jobs.
I want drivers involved before **robot orders** are signed.
think: At 51 in 2034, I may still owe on the **mortgage** and support older children.
Nearby mines offer options, but a **classroom trade** does not appeal to me.
do: Ask the union for **paid mechanical training** and a wage floor.
Enrol if paid time is secured while **keeping truck shifts**.
Check 2032 driver numbers and apply to **other mines** if ours shrinks.
feel: **Steadier** with time to bargain, though still wary of unpaid study.
S3.quote: I still dislike being told to retrain as if the mortgage will pause during a course.
fieldNote: Liam’s resistance to new tools softens only for **paid, supervised mechanical work**.
He connects collective bargaining to a **written wage floor** rather than an abstract demand for fairness.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for paid mechanical training and a wage floor
Enrol in supervised mechanical inspection if paid release time is secured
Keep current truck shifts during any paid course
Apply to nearby mines in 2032 if driver numbers shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that ten years is enough to put terms in a proper agreement. Thinking AI changes the office in 2036; robots capable of driving our trucks follow around 2039. Nobody should call a driver safe forever, but nobody needs to resign tomorrow either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when the thinking AI arrives and 56 when the robots arrive. Our children should be grown by then, so their bus passes and school outings won't be our weekly bills. I have savings and plenty of nearby mines, but I don't know the mortgage balance or what paid work will be there at 56. I'm not counting on a pension I haven't checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the truck job now and ask the union for a yearly report on robot orders and driver vacancies. This winter Sam and I would review the mortgage balance and put more of my higher wage toward the principal if our regular bills allow. In 2037 I'd still drive while checking the job board at nearby mines and the mine’s paid inspection vacancies. Before 2039 I'd apply for an inspection opening if it offered real wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered with a decade, though I won't call it calm. A good savings balance today doesn't guarantee a wage twelve or thirteen years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know whether we could afford it. I'd check the pension statement and the mortgage before saying that; 56 isn't an automatic finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in that yearly report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many trucks are ordered, what jobs are being removed, and what the replacement jobs pay. If the numbers are hidden, the ten years can disappear while we argue.

say: I would say a **ten-year runway** gives drivers time to negotiate proper terms.
Office AI in **2036** and truck robots around 2039 need separate plans.
think: At 56, my grown children may cost less, but **mortgage and wages** remain uncertain.
I will not assume a **pension** can replace work without checking it.
do: Keep driving and request a **yearly robot report** through the union.
Review the mortgage with Sam and make extra **principal payments** if bills allow.
Check vacancies in 2037 and apply for **paid inspection work** before 2039.
feel: Less **cornered**, but unwilling to call future wages secure.
S4.quote: A good savings balance today doesn't guarantee a wage twelve or thirteen years from now.
fieldNote: His decade plan combines **union transparency** with a household mortgage review.
He does not assume grown children keep school costs, or that **retirement at 56** is funded.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck while work remains available
Request yearly robot order and vacancy reports through the union
Pay extra mortgage principal if regular bills allow
Apply for paid mine inspection openings before 2039

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 one worries me most. A written driver plan, paid training time and a wage floor would give me something to take home to Sam. The savings are there, but I don't want to spend them while management decides whether I still have a seat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets to see the numbers before a robot contract is signed. A driver can only plan around a date the mine is willing to put on paper. The mine’s silence can use up the very years we’re told we have.

headlineQuote: The mine’s silence can use up the very years we’re told we have.
portrait: Liam is a **43-year-old junior driver** on higher mine pay, with two school-age children and a mortgage.
His **strong savings** soften a job shock, while Sam’s variable school kitchen hours keep household risk alive.
He prefers familiar **paper routes** and never uses AI, yet he will consider paid mechanical instruction.
He seeks **union records** and a wage floor before robot orders turn into lost truck shifts.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because capable truck robots follow around 2031, leaving little time to secure paid work.
whatWouldHelp: A **written driver plan**, paid training time and a wage floor would make the transition credible.
